# Ch.5 — Replication

**Source:** `ddia_kleppmann` (Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017)
**PDF page range:** 167–212 (46 pages) — per `audit/CHAPTER_MAP.csv`
**Chapter map status:** `located`, `entry_type: chapter`
**Synthesis status:** `synthesized` (this session)
**Provenance key:** `[S]` source-supported · `[D]` derived interpretation · `[U]` unresolved

---

## 1. Concepts and definitions

**Replication, defined and its three named motivations [S]** (p167): "keeping a copy of the same data on multiple machines that are connected via a network." Named reasons: geographic proximity to users (lower latency), continued operation despite partial failure (availability), and scaling read throughput across machines.

**Leader-based replication, the chapter's own three-rule mechanism [S]** (p168–169): one replica is the leader (master/primary) — clients must send writes to it; the other replicas are followers (read replicas/slaves/hot standbys) — the leader sends every write to them "as part of a replication log or change stream," and each follower applies writes "in the same order as they were processed on the leader"; clients may read from the leader or any follower, but "writes are only accepted on the leader."

**Synchronous vs. asynchronous replication, precisely distinguished [S]** (p169–171): synchronous means "the leader waits until follower 1 has confirmed that it received the write before reporting success to the user"; asynchronous means "the leader sends the message, but doesn't wait for a response." Fully synchronous replication to all followers is named impractical: "any one node outage would cause the whole system to grind to a halt." The common compromise is semi-synchronous: exactly one follower is synchronous (promoted from the asynchronous pool if it becomes unavailable), guaranteeing an up-to-date copy on "at least two nodes: the leader and one synchronous follower."

**Setting up a new follower, the chapter's own four-step procedure [S]** (p171): take a consistent snapshot of the leader without locking the whole database; copy the snapshot to the new node; the follower requests all changes since the snapshot's exact log position (PostgreSQL's log sequence number, MySQL's binlog coordinates); the follower applies the backlog and "has caught up."

**Failover, defined and its three-step automatic procedure [S]** (p172–173): "one of the followers needs to be promoted to be the new leader, clients need to be reconfigured to send their writes to the new leader, and the other followers need to start consuming data changes from the new leader." Automatic failover: (1) detect leader failure, almost always via a timeout heuristic since "there is no foolproof way of detecting what has gone wrong"; (2) choose a new leader, either by election among replicas or via a pre-elected controller, favoring the replica with the most up-to-date data; (3) reconfigure clients and ensure the old leader steps down to follower if it rejoins.

**Split brain, defined and named dangerous [S]** (p173): the situation "when two nodes both believe that they are the leader" — if both accept writes with no conflict-resolution process, "data is likely to be lost or corrupted." Some systems use fencing/STONITH ("Shoot The Other Node In The Head") to shut one node down when this is detected.

**Statement-based, WAL-shipping, and logical (row-based) log replication, three named implementation methods with distinct trade-offs [S]** (p175): statement-based forwards the literal SQL statement and breaks on non-determinism (`NOW()`, `RAND()`), auto-increment/order dependence, and non-deterministic triggers/UDFs. WAL shipping reuses the storage engine's own write-ahead log, giving a very compact and exact replication mechanism, but couples replication tightly to storage-engine internals — "if the database changes its storage format from one version to another, it is typically not possible to run different versions of the database software on the leader and the followers" (p175), blocking zero-downtime upgrades. Logical log replication decouples the replication format from storage internals (row-level insert/update/delete records), remaining backward-compatible across software/storage-engine versions and enabling change data capture for external consumers (data warehouses, custom indexes).

**Trigger-based replication, defined by its flexibility-for-overhead trade [S]** (p177): implemented at the application layer via database triggers/stored procedures rather than as a database-engine built-in; needed for partial replication, cross-database-type replication, or custom conflict resolution, but has "greater overheads... and is more prone to bugs and limitations than the database's built-in replication."

**Eventual consistency, precisely scoped [S]** (p177): the temporary inconsistency visible when reading from an asynchronous follower that has fallen behind — "if you stop writing to the database and wait a while, the followers will eventually catch up and become consistent with the leader." "The term eventually is deliberately vague: in general, there is no limit how far a replica can fall behind."

**Read-after-write (read-your-writes) consistency, defined [S]** (p178): "a guarantee that if the user reloads the page, they will always see any updates they submitted themselves." It makes no promise about visibility of other users' writes.

Four named implementation techniques for read-after-write consistency, synthesized from the chapter's own list (p178–179) `[D]`: read user-modifiable data from the leader and everything else from followers; time-since-last-update or replica-lag thresholds to decide leader-vs-follower routing; client-remembered write timestamps (logical or wall-clock) that a chosen replica must have caught up to before serving the read; and datacenter-routing consistency for multi-device cross-device read-after-write.

**Monotonic reads, defined and distinguished from eventual/strong consistency [S]** (p180): "a guarantee that this kind of anomaly does not happen" where "a user sees things moving backwards in time" across successive reads from replicas at different lag. "It's a lesser guarantee than strong consistency, but a stronger guarantee than eventual consistency." Implemented by routing each user consistently to the same replica (e.g. via a hash of user ID).

**Consistent prefix reads, defined via the Mr Poons/Mrs Cake causality example [S]** (p182): the guarantee "that if a sequence of writes happens in a certain order, then anyone reading those writes will see them appear in the same order" — preventing an observer from seeing an answer replicated before the question that caused it, a problem specific to partitioned databases where "different partitions operate independently, so there is no global ordering of writes."

**Multi-leader replication, defined and its core downside named [S]** (p183): more than one node accepts writes, each forwarding its changes to all others, with "each leader simultaneously acts as a follower to the other leaders." Named downside: "the same data may be concurrently modified in two different datacenters, and those write conflicts must be resolved."

**Three named legitimate multi-leader use cases [S]** (p188–191): multi-datacenter operation (each datacenter has a local leader, hiding inter-datacenter latency from users, and tolerating both datacenter outages and inter-datacenter network problems better than single-leader); clients with offline operation (each device is effectively its own "datacenter" with a local leader, syncing asynchronously — calendar apps as the worked example); real-time collaborative editing (Etherpad/Google Docs), which the chapter explicitly reframes as "essentially the same as multi-leader replication between datacenters, taken to the extreme."

**Write conflicts, the biggest multi-leader problem [S]** (p186): illustrated via two users concurrently retitling the same wiki page on different leaders — "this problem does not occur in a single-leader database."

Making conflict detection synchronous would (p187) "lose the main advantage of multi-leader replication: allowing each replica to accept writes independently." Most conflicts are therefore detected only after the fact, asynchronously. `[D]`

**Four named convergent conflict-resolution techniques [S]** (p188): assign each write a unique ID (timestamp/random/UUID/hash) and let the highest-ID write win — "last write wins" (LWW). This technique is "dangerously prone to data loss" (p188). Giving each replica a fixed priority ranking "also implies data loss" (p188); merge values (e.g. alphabetical concatenation); or record the conflict explicitly and resolve it later, possibly via the user.

**Custom conflict resolution's two execution points, on write vs. on read [S]** (p189): on-write handlers (e.g. Bucardo's Perl snippets) run in a background process and cannot prompt a user; on-read approaches (CouchDB's model) surface all conflicting versions to the application at the next read, letting it prompt the user or auto-resolve.

**CRDTs, mergeable persistent data structures, and operational transformation, three named automatic-conflict-resolution research lines [S]** (p189): CRDTs (Riak 2.0) automatically resolve concurrent set/map/list/counter edits via two-way merges; mergeable persistent data structures track history like git and use three-way merges; operational transformation is the algorithm behind Etherpad/Google Docs, designed specifically for concurrently edited ordered lists of characters.

**Replication topology, defined, with three named shapes and their fault-tolerance trade-off [S]** (p191): circular (each node forwards to exactly one other, e.g. MySQL's default), star (one root forwards to all others, generalizable to a tree), and all-to-all (every leader sends to every other). Circular/star topologies are vulnerable to a single node's failure interrupting the whole forwarding chain; all-to-all is more fault-tolerant but can suffer message reordering when some network links are faster than others, with some replication messages effectively overtaking others in transit (p191). `[D]`

**Leaderless replication, defined by its Dynamo lineage and its abandonment of write ordering [S]** (p200): "any replica to directly accept writes from clients," popularized by Amazon's internal Dynamo system and its open-source descendants (Riak, Cassandra, Voldemort — "Dynamo-style"). Unlike a leader, a coordinator (if used) "does not enforce a particular ordering of writes."

**Quorum reads and writes, the chapter's own n/w/r formalism [S]** (p195): "if there are n replicas, every write must be confirmed by w nodes to be considered successful, and we must query at least r nodes for each read... As long as w + r > n, we expect to get an up-to-date value when reading, because at least one of the r nodes we're reading from must be up-to-date." A common configuration sets n odd (3 or 5) and w = r = (n+1)/2 rounded up.

**Six named edge cases where quorums still return stale values despite w+r>n [S]** (p197–198): sloppy quorums breaking the guaranteed w/r node overlap; concurrent writes with no defined "first" requiring a merge, or unsafe timestamp-based LWW under clock skew; a write concurrent with a read leaving it undetermined which value the read returns; a partially-failed write (succeeded on fewer than w replicas) not being rolled back; a node restored from a stale replica dropping the surviving-copy count of a value below w; and generic distributed-timing unluckiness deferred to the linearizability discussion in a later chapter.

**Sloppy quorum and hinted handoff, defined via the borrow-your-neighbor's-couch analogy [S]** (p199): during a network interruption, the database may "accept writes anyway, and write them to some nodes that are reachable but aren't among the n nodes on which the value usually lives" — this is a sloppy quorum. Once connectivity is restored, those borrowed writes are forwarded to their proper "home" nodes: hinted handoff. Explicit consequence: "a sloppy quorum actually isn't a quorum at all in the traditional sense. It's only an assurance of durability."

**The "happens-before" relationship, the chapter's own general definition of concurrency [S]** (p202): "An operation A happens before another operation B if B knows about A, or depends on A, or builds upon A in some way." "In fact, we can simply say that two operations are concurrent if neither happens before the other, i.e. neither knows about the other" (p202). Explicitly decoupled from wall-clock simultaneity, with an explicit analogy to relativistic causality (information cannot outrun the events that caused it).

**Last write wins (LWW), the chapter's own durability-cost warning and its one safe usage pattern [S]** (p202): forces an arbitrary total order via timestamps, discarding all but the highest; "achieves the goal of eventual convergence, but at the cost of durability" since concurrent writes not written last are "silently discarded." The only safe usage the chapter names: write each key exactly once and treat it as immutable thereafter (e.g. UUID-keyed writes in Cassandra), eliminating concurrent updates to the same key entirely.

**Per-key version numbers, the chapter's own single-replica algorithm for tracking siblings [S]** (p205–206): the server increments a per-key version number on every write; a client must read (and receive the current version plus all not-yet-overwritten values) before writing; a write must include the version from that prior read and must merge all values the client received; the server then overwrites everything at or below the submitted version but must keep any value with a higher version as a concurrent sibling.

**Version vectors, the multi-replica generalization [S]** (p207): "a version number per replica as well as per key" — each replica tracks both its own counter and the counters it has seen from every other replica, letting it distinguish overwrites from concurrent siblings without relying on a single global counter. A named variant, the dotted version vector, is used in Riak 2.0.

## 2. WHAT / WHY / WHEN

**WHAT:** the chapter's full taxonomy of replication algorithms — single-leader, multi-leader, and leaderless — organized around one recurring question: given that "all writes must go through the same replica" is not always survivable or fast enough, how does a system reconcile multiple copies of changing data while defining precisely what consistency guarantee (if any) a reader gets. `[D]`

**WHY it matters:** replication's difficulty is entirely about handling *changes* to data over time — "if the data that you're replicating does not change over time, then replication is easy" (p167) — so every technique in the chapter (log formats, quorum parameters, conflict-resolution rules, causality tracking) exists specifically to answer what a reader may legitimately see while writes are still propagating, which is the practical substance behind the abstract term "eventual consistency." `[D]`

**WHEN to choose leader-based vs. multi-leader vs. leaderless, synthesized across the chapter (p167–207):** use single-leader when a simple, strongly-ordered write path within one datacenter is acceptable and read-scaling via asynchronous followers is enough; use multi-leader specifically for multi-datacenter write locality, offline-capable clients, or real-time collaborative editing, accepting the added cost of conflict resolution; use leaderless (Dynamo-style) when high write availability and tunable staleness under partial node failure matter more than any ordering guarantee, and the application can tolerate or explicitly merge sibling values. `[D]`

## 3. Assumptions and prerequisites

- Assumes the dataset is small enough that every node holds a full copy — explicitly deferred to Ch.6 (Partitioning) for datasets too large for one machine. `[S]` (p167)
- Assumes and directly reuses Ch.3's storage-engine internals (LSM-tree compaction log, B-tree write-ahead log) as the substrate for WAL-shipping replication. `[S]` (p176)
- Assumes and directly reuses Ch.4's encoding/decoding vocabulary implicitly (row-based logical logs as a form of change-data-capture encoding), forward-referencing Ch.11 for the full CDC treatment. `[D]`
- Forward-references transaction serializability and snapshot isolation to Ch.7, unreliable-clock and timing-fault detail to Ch.8, and the consensus problem (leader election) and linearizability-quorum edge cases to Ch.9 — all not yet synthesized in this vault. `[D]`

## 4. Mechanism / key steps

**Semi-synchronous replication's self-healing configuration, synthesized from the chapter's own description (p170)** `[D]`: enable synchronous replication on exactly one follower → if that follower becomes unavailable or slow, promote one of the asynchronous followers to synchronous in its place → this guarantees an up-to-date copy always exists on at least two nodes (leader + current synchronous follower) without ever blocking on all followers simultaneously.

**Read-repair mechanism, the chapter's own worked description (p194)** `[D]`: a leaderless read is sent to several replicas in parallel → the client (or coordinator) compares the version numbers/values returned → any replica returning a stale value is sent the newer value directly by the client, on the spot → this only heals values that are actually read, motivating the separate anti-entropy background process for rarely-read keys.

**Sibling-tracking write protocol, the chapter's own five-client shopping-cart worked example (p203–204)** `[D]`: client reads a key, receiving all current (non-overwritten) values plus the latest version number → client merges those values with its own new item → client writes back the merged value tagged with the version number it read → server overwrites every value at or below that version (now known to be merged in) but preserves any value at a higher version as a concurrent sibling → repeat; the true current state is the client-merged union of all outstanding siblings until further overwrites resolve them.

## 5. Trade-offs and limitations

- **Synchronous replication guarantees an up-to-date follower at the cost of write availability; fully asynchronous replication trades durability for continuous write processing (§1, p169–171):** an explicit, direct trade the chapter resolves via the semi-synchronous compromise rather than picking one extreme.
- **WAL-shipping replication is compact and exact but couples the leader and follower to the same storage-engine version, blocking zero-downtime software upgrades; logical log replication decouples this at the cost of a separate log format to maintain (§1, p178–179):** a genuine two-sided trade with no dominant option.
- **Multi-leader replication buys write locality and datacenter/network fault tolerance at the direct cost of needing conflict resolution — a cost the chapter names as often not worth it "within a single datacenter" (§1, p188):** multi-leader is explicitly framed as justified only by specific use cases (multi-datacenter, offline clients, collaborative editing), not a general-purpose upgrade over single-leader.
- **Last write wins achieves convergence but is "dangerously prone to data loss" — a durability cost the chapter treats as acceptable only for caching-like workloads or immutable-key usage patterns (§1, p194, p211–212):** not a neutral default; a deliberate risk trade that must be scoped narrowly.
- **Sloppy quorums increase write availability during network partitions but break the very w+r>n overlap guarantee that quorums are supposed to provide (§1, p207):** an explicit, named contradiction the chapter states outright — "a sloppy quorum actually isn't a quorum at all in the traditional sense."

## 6. Failure modes and edge cases

- **GitHub's primary-key-reuse incident during failover (§1, p173):** a promoted, lagging MySQL follower reused auto-increment primary keys already assigned by the old leader; because those keys were also referenced in a separate Redis store, the collision "resulted in inconsistency between MySQL and Redis, which caused some private data to be disclosed to the wrong users" — a concrete, named cross-system data-loss consequence of naive failover.
- **Split-brain double-shutdown (§1, p173):** the chapter names the risk that a fencing/STONITH mechanism can itself misfire, leaving "both nodes being shut down" — a failure mode of the very safety mechanism meant to prevent split-brain damage.
- **Statement-based replication's non-determinism failures (§1, p176):** `NOW()`/`RAND()` calls, auto-increment/order-dependent statements executed out of order, and non-deterministic triggers/UDFs are each named as concrete ways this replication method silently diverges follower state from the leader.
- **Amazon's shopping-cart conflict-resolution bug (§1, p196):** a real, named production incident where a custom conflict handler preserved added items but not removed items, causing "customers would sometimes see items re-appearing in their cart even though they had previously been removed" — a concrete illustration of how error-prone hand-written conflict resolution is.
- **Union-merge of siblings silently resurrecting deleted items (§1, p215):** if an item is removed from only one sibling cart, a naive union-merge of siblings brings it back — motivating the tombstone marker pattern rather than plain deletion.

## 7. Implications for design / build / maintain / RCA / optimization

- **Design:** the single-leader / multi-leader / leaderless decision framework (§2) is directly reusable as a first-pass architecture decision for any new replicated data store in this vault's projects — start from the use case (write locality need, offline tolerance, staleness tolerance) rather than defaulting to whichever model is most familiar. `[D]`
- **Build:** the semi-synchronous replication configuration pattern (§4, p170) is a directly reusable durability/availability compromise for any leader-based system where full synchronous replication to all followers is judged too fragile.
- **Maintain:** the read-after-write and monotonic-reads implementation techniques (§1, p181–184) are directly reusable operational patterns for diagnosing and fixing "my own write disappeared" or "data went backwards" user-facing bug reports against an asynchronously replicated read path.
- **RCA:** an observed data-loss or reappearing-data incident in a multi-leader or leaderless system is directly diagnosable against the chapter's named conflict-resolution failure patterns (§6) — check for LWW discarding a concurrent write, or a naive union-merge resurrecting a deletion, before assuming an application bug.
- **Optimization:** the quorum n/w/r tuning framework (§1, p202–205) is a directly reusable lever for trading staleness probability against latency and availability in any leaderless-style datastore — favoring smaller w/r for lower latency and higher availability, larger w/r for stronger read-your-writes-like guarantees.

## 8. How to test / verify these claims

- The synchronous-vs-asynchronous replication lag behavior (§1, p169–171) is directly reproducible: configure a database (e.g. PostgreSQL) with one synchronous and one asynchronous follower, kill the asynchronous follower's network connection, and confirm writes still succeed while the synchronous path continues to block correctly if that follower is killed instead.
- The quorum condition w+r>n (§1, p202) is directly testable by construction: set up a 3-node Dynamo-style store (e.g. Cassandra) with n=3, w=2, r=2, take one node offline, and confirm writes and reads both continue to succeed while consistency is (usually) preserved.
- The sibling-version-tracking algorithm (§4, p213–216) is directly reproducible: implement the shopping-cart worked example against a real Riak (or equivalent) cluster, deliberately interleaving concurrent writes from two clients, and confirm that the returned sibling set matches the chapter's Figure 5-13 trace.
- The LWW data-loss claim (§1, p211–212) is directly testable: issue two concurrent writes to the same key in a Cassandra table with default LWW conflict resolution, and confirm one write is silently discarded rather than surfaced as a conflict.

## 9. Cross-references

- Directly extends Ch.3's storage-engine log mechanics (LSM-tree, B-tree WAL) as the concrete substrate for WAL-shipping replication — no contradiction found. `[D]`
- Directly extends Ch.4's discussion of backward/forward compatibility: WAL shipping's storage-engine coupling is the same compatibility problem Ch.4 discusses in the abstract, now applied specifically to replication protocols across software versions. `[D]`
- Forward-references (not yet synthesized in this vault): Ch.6 (partitioning of datasets too large for one machine), Ch.7 (transactions, snapshot isolation, and the consistent-prefix-reads causal-transaction connection), Ch.8 (unreliable clocks and network timing faults underlying failover-timeout and LWW-clock-skew issues), Ch.9 (leader-election consensus and linearizability/quorum edge cases), and Ch.11 (full change-data-capture treatment building on this chapter's logical-log replication).
- No contradiction found with any already-synthesized source in this vault.

# Ch.6 — Partitioning

**Source:** `ddia_kleppmann` (Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017)
**PDF page range:** 213–234 (22 pages) — per `audit/CHAPTER_MAP.csv`
**Chapter map status:** `located`, `entry_type: chapter`
**Synthesis status:** `synthesized` (this session)
**Provenance key:** `[S]` source-supported · `[D]` derived interpretation · `[U]` unresolved

---

## 1. Concepts and definitions

**Partitioning, defined [S]** (p213): "a way of intentionally breaking a large database down into smaller ones."

An explicit footnote warns this has (p213) "nothing to do with network partitions (netsplits), a type of fault in the network between nodes" — deferred to Ch.8.

**Skew and hot spots, precisely defined [S]** (p215): "If the partitioning is unfair, so that some partitions have more data or queries than others, we call it skewed." "A partition with disproportionately high load is called a hot spot." In the extreme, "nine out of ten nodes are idle, and your bottleneck is the single busy node."

**Key-range partitioning, defined via the paper-encyclopedia analogy [S]** (p215–216): "assign a continuous range of keys (from some minimum to some maximum) to each partition, like the volumes of a paper encyclopedia." Range boundaries "are not necessarily evenly spaced, because your data may not be evenly distributed" — they "need to adapt to the data" to distribute it evenly, chosen either manually or automatically.

**Key-range partitioning's range-scan advantage, worked via a sensor-timestamp example [S]** (p216–217): "we can keep keys in sorted order... range scans are easy" — e.g. fetching all readings from a given month directly. But if the key is a raw timestamp, "all the writes end up going to the same partition (the one for today), so that partition can be overloaded with writes while others sit idle." Fix: prefix the timestamp with a discriminating field (e.g. sensor name) so writes spread across partitions, at the cost of needing a separate range query per discriminator.

**Hash partitioning, defined and its trade-off named directly [S]** (p217–218): "a good hash function takes skewed data and makes it uniformly distributed" — assigning each partition a range of hashes rather than a range of keys. "This technique is good at distributing keys fairly among the partitions," but "we also lost a nice property of key-range partitioning: the ability to do efficient range queries" (p218) since "keys that were once adjacent are now scattered across all the partitions."

**Consistent hashing, precisely scoped and explicitly named a confusing misnomer for databases [S]** (p218): "a way of evenly distributing load across an internet-wide system of caches, such as a CDN," using randomly chosen boundaries to avoid central coordination. "This particular approach actually doesn't work very well for databases... so it is rarely used in practice." The chapter's own recommendation: "it's best to avoid the term consistent hashing, and just call it hash partitioning instead."

**Cassandra's compound-key compromise between key-range and hash partitioning [S]** (p218–219): only the first part of a compound primary key is hashed to pick the partition; the remaining columns form a concatenated sort index within that partition. Worked example: with primary key `(user_id, update_timestamp)`, "you can efficiently retrieve all updates made by a particular user within some time interval, sorted by timestamp" (p218), while different users are spread across different partitions.

**Skewed workloads that hashing cannot fix, the celebrity-user worked example [S]** (p219–220): "in the extreme case where all reads and writes are for the same key, you still end up with all requests being routed to the same partition" — "hashing the key doesn't help, as the hash of two identical IDs is still the same." Named mitigation: append a small random number (e.g. two digits) to a known-hot key, splitting its writes across 100 keys, at the cost of reads needing to fan out and combine all 100, plus bookkeeping to know which keys were split.

**Document-partitioned (local) secondary indexes, defined via the used-car-listing example [S]** (p220–221): "each partition maintains its own secondary indexes, covering only the documents in that partition." Writes touch only one partition, but "reading from a document-partitioned index requires care" — since matching records can be scattered across partitions, a query must "send the query to all partitions, and combine all the results" — a pattern named scatter/gather, which "is prone to tail latency amplification."

**Term-partitioned (global) secondary indexes, defined and their write/read trade-off directly stated [S]** (p222): "a global index... can be partitioned differently from the primary key index," partitioned either by the term itself (useful for range scans) or by a hash of the term (more even load). Advantage: "a client only needs to make a request to the partition containing the term that it wants" for reads. Named downside: "writes are now slower and more complicated, because a write to a single document may now affect multiple partitions of the index."

**Global secondary index update latency, an explicit consistency caveat [S]** (p222): keeping a term-partitioned index perfectly up to date would require "a distributed transaction across all partitions affected by a write, which is not supported in all databases"

In practice (p222), "updates to global secondary indexes are often asynchronous" — Amazon DynamoDB is named as updating within a fraction of a second normally, but potentially experiencing longer propagation delays in case of infrastructure faults. `[D]`

**Rebalancing, defined and its three named minimum requirements [S]** (p223): "the process of moving data around between nodes in the cluster is called rebalancing." After rebalancing, load should be shared fairly; during rebalancing, the database should keep accepting reads and writes; and rebalancing should not move more data than necessary.

**Hash-mod-N rebalancing, explicitly named the wrong approach, with a worked numeric example [S]** (p223–224): "the problem with the mod N approach is that if the number of nodes N changes, most of the keys would need to be moved from one node to another." Worked example: `hash(key)=123456` moves from node 6 (mod 10) to node 3 (mod 11) to node 0 (mod 12) as the cluster grows by one node at a time — "that makes rebalancing excessively expensive."

**Fixed number of partitions, the chapter's own preferred rebalancing strategy for hash partitioning [S]** (p224): "create many more partitions than there are nodes, and assign several partitions to each node" (e.g. 1,000 partitions across 10 nodes). Adding a node lets it "steal a few partitions from every existing node." Crucially, "only entire partitions are moved between nodes... the assignment of keys to partitions does not change" — only which node owns which partition. This also allows manually weighting more powerful nodes with more partitions.

**Dynamic partitioning, the chapter's own mechanism for key-range partitioning [S]** (p225): "when a partition grows to exceed a configured size... it is split into two partitions so that approximately half of the data ends up on each side of the split," and shrinking, deleted-heavy partitions "can be merged with an adjacent partition" — explicitly likened to B-tree node splitting/merging.

**Pre-splitting, a named mitigation for dynamic partitioning's cold-start problem [S]** (p226): "an empty database starts off with a single partition... all writes have to be processed by a single node while the other nodes sit idle" until the first split. HBase and MongoDB let an administrator configure an initial partition set on an empty database to avoid this.

**Automatic vs. manual rebalancing, an explicit availability-vs-safety trade-off with a named cascading-failure risk [S]** (p226–227): fully automatic rebalancing reduces operational burden but "can be unpredictable" and dangerous when combined with automatic failure detection — "one node is overloaded and is temporarily slow to respond... the other nodes conclude that the overloaded node is dead, and automatically rebalance the cluster to move load away from it," which can overload the remaining nodes and "cause a cascading failure." The chapter's own conclusion: "it can be a good thing to have a human in the loop for rebalancing."

**Request routing, defined as an instance of the general service-discovery problem, with three named approaches [S]** (p227–228): (1) let clients contact any node via a load balancer, and have that node forward the request if it doesn't own the relevant partition; (2) send all requests through a dedicated routing tier that itself does no data processing; (3) require clients to be partition-aware and connect directly to the correct node. In all three, "the key problem is: how does the component making the routing decision... learn about changes in the assignment of partitions to nodes?"

**ZooKeeper-based cluster metadata coordination, the chapter's own worked description [S]** (p228): "many distributed data systems rely on a separate coordination service such as ZooKeeper to keep track of this cluster metadata"

"Each node registers itself in ZooKeeper, and ZooKeeper maintains the authoritative mapping of partitions to nodes" (p228), notifying subscribed routing tiers or clients on any change. LinkedIn's Espresso (via Helix), HBase, SolrCloud, and Kafka are named examples; MongoDB uses its own config-server equivalent instead.

**Gossip-protocol routing, Cassandra/Riak's alternative to a coordination service [S]** (p229): nodes "use a gossip protocol among the nodes to disseminate and agree on any changes in cluster state," letting requests be sent to any node which then forwards internally — "this puts more complexity in the database nodes, but avoids the dependency on an external coordination service such as ZooKeeper."

## 2. WHAT / WHY / WHEN

**WHAT:** the chapter's full taxonomy of ways to split a single logical dataset across many machines — key-range vs. hash partitioning of primary data, document- vs. term-partitioned secondary indexes, and the rebalancing/routing machinery needed to keep such a partitioned system correct and load-balanced as nodes are added or removed. `[D]`

**WHY it matters:** replication (Ch.5) alone cannot help once a dataset or its query throughput exceeds what a single machine can store or serve; partitioning is explicitly framed as replication's complement — "for very large datasets, or very high query throughput, that is not sufficient: we also need to break the data up into partitions" (p213) — and the two concerns compose independently, since "the choice of partitioning scheme is mostly independent of the choice of replication scheme" (p214). `[S]`

**WHEN to choose key-range vs. hash partitioning (p215–219, synthesized across the chapter):** favor key-range partitioning when efficient range scans on the primary key are a first-class requirement (e.g. time-series data queried by date range), accepting the risk of write hot spots on monotonically increasing keys unless mitigated (e.g. prefixing with a discriminator); favor hash partitioning when even load distribution matters more than range-scan support, accepting that range queries on the primary key become a full scatter/gather or are unsupported entirely.

**WHEN to choose document-partitioned vs. term-partitioned secondary indexes (p220–223, synthesized across the chapter):** favor document-partitioned (local) indexes when writes must stay cheap and single-partition, and read-side scatter/gather latency is acceptable; favor term-partitioned (global) indexes when secondary-index reads must be served from a single partition and the workload can tolerate both slower, multi-partition writes and (in most real systems) asynchronous index staleness.

## 3. Assumptions and prerequisites

- Directly extends Ch.5's replication material, explicitly stating the two concerns are independent and that "everything we discussed in Chapter 5 about replication of databases applies equally to replication of partitions" — this chapter deliberately ignores replication to isolate partitioning concerns. `[S]` (p214)
- Assumes and directly reuses Ch.3's B-tree and SSTable/LSM-tree sorted-storage mechanics, both for within-partition key ordering under key-range partitioning and for the dynamic-partitioning split/merge analogy to B-tree nodes. `[S]` (p216, p225)
- Forward-references distributed transactions across partitions to Ch.7 (the chapter's own footnote iii points to its "multi-object transactions" section), and distributed consensus protocols underlying reliable request routing to Ch.9 — both not yet synthesized in this vault. `[D]`
- Forward-references parallel query execution techniques for data-warehouse-style analytics to Ch.10 — not yet synthesized in this vault. `[D]`

## 4. Mechanism / key steps

**Fixed-number-of-partitions rebalancing procedure, the chapter's own worked description (p224)** `[D]`: at cluster setup, create a partition count much larger than the expected node count (e.g. 1,000 partitions for 10 nodes) → assign a roughly even share of partitions to each node → when a node is added, it takes over a few partitions from each existing node until the distribution is even again → when a node is removed, its partitions are redistributed to the remaining nodes → throughout, the assignment of individual keys to partitions never changes, only the assignment of whole partitions to nodes, keeping data movement proportional to the rebalancing delta rather than the full dataset.

**Dynamic partitioning's split/merge cycle for key-range partitioning, the chapter's own worked description (p225)** `[D]`: a partition accumulates writes until it exceeds a configured size threshold (e.g. 10GB on HBase) → the partition is split into two, each covering half the original key range → one half may be transferred to a different node to rebalance load, moved via the underlying distributed filesystem (e.g. HDFS for HBase) → conversely, if deletions shrink a partition below a threshold, it can be merged back with an adjacent partition.

## 5. Trade-offs and limitations

- **Key-range partitioning enables efficient range scans but is vulnerable to write hot spots on sequentially increasing keys; hash partitioning distributes load evenly but destroys range-scan efficiency entirely (§1, p216–218):** a direct, unavoidable two-sided trade with no dominant strategy — Cassandra's compound-key compromise (§1, p218–219) only partially resolves it by hashing just the first key component.
- **Document-partitioned secondary indexes keep writes cheap (single partition) but make reads expensive (scatter/gather across all partitions); term-partitioned (global) indexes make reads cheap (single partition) but make writes expensive (potentially many partitions touched) (§1, p220–222):** an explicit, named inversion of the same cost between the two approaches.
- **Fully automatic rebalancing reduces operational toil but risks a cascading failure when combined with automatic failure detection under load (§1, p226–227):** the chapter explicitly favors a human-in-the-loop compromise over full automation, trading operational speed for safety.
- **A fixed number of partitions is operationally simple but caps the maximum future cluster size and wastes overhead if set too high; dynamic partitioning removes that cap but suffers a cold-start single-partition bottleneck on an empty database unless pre-split (§1, p224–226):** neither strategy dominates — the choice depends on whether the workload needs key-range partitioning (which favors dynamic) or hash partitioning (which favors fixed).

## 6. Failure modes and edge cases

- **Celebrity-user hot spots surviving hash partitioning entirely (§1, p219–220):** a real, named production pattern — "a celebrity user with millions of followers may cause a storm of activity" — where hashing provides zero mitigation because the hash of one repeatedly-written key is always the same value, routing every request to the same partition regardless of hash quality.
- **Global secondary index staleness after a write (§1, p223):** a read of a term-partitioned index shortly after a write may not yet reflect that write, since most real systems update global indexes asynchronously rather than transactionally — a concrete, named eventual-consistency gap distinct from the primary-key data path.
- **Automatic-rebalancing-triggered cascading failure (§1, p226–227):** a temporarily overloaded (not actually dead) node gets misdiagnosed as failed by automatic health checks, triggering an automatic rebalance that shifts more load onto already-strained remaining nodes, "potentially overloading more nodes and causing a cascading failure" — a self-inflicted failure mode of the automation meant to prevent downtime.
- **Application-implemented secondary indexes drifting out of sync with primary data (§1, p220, footnote iii):** if a database supports only key-value access and an application hand-rolls a value-to-ID index mapping itself, "race conditions and intermittent write failures... can very easily cause the data to go out of sync" — deferred explicitly to Ch.7's multi-object transaction discussion.

## 7. Implications for design / build / maintain / RCA / optimization

- **Design:** the key-range-vs-hash and document-vs-term-index decision frameworks (§2) are directly reusable as first-pass sharding-strategy decisions for any new partitioned datastore in this vault's projects, driven by whether range scans on the partition key are a real workload requirement. `[D]`
- **Build:** the fixed-number-of-partitions rebalancing pattern (§4, p224) is a directly reusable design choice for any hash-partitioned system anticipating future node growth — provisioning partition count well above the expected eventual node count avoids the hash-mod-N rebalancing trap.
- **Maintain:** the pre-splitting mitigation (§1, p226) is a directly reusable operational technique for any dynamically-partitioned system where the expected key distribution is knowable in advance, avoiding the empty-database single-node bottleneck.
- **RCA:** a cluster observed to enter escalating overload immediately after a partial node slowdown is directly diagnosable against the automatic-rebalancing cascading-failure pattern (§6, p226–227) — check whether automatic rebalancing was triggered by a false-positive failure detection before assuming a capacity problem.
- **Optimization:** the document-vs-term secondary-index trade-off (§1, p220–222) is a directly reusable lever for tuning read/write cost balance in any partitioned system with secondary indexes — favor document-partitioned indexes for write-heavy workloads, term-partitioned for read-heavy ones where read latency dominates.

## 8. How to test / verify these claims

- The hash-mod-N rebalancing cost claim (§1, p223–224) is directly reproducible: compute `hash(key) mod N` for a fixed key across N=10, 11, 12 and confirm the assigned node changes almost every time, versus a fixed-partition-count scheme where only whole-partition ownership moves.
- The document-partitioned scatter/gather read cost (§1, p221) is directly testable: populate a document-partitioned datastore (e.g. MongoDB or Elasticsearch) across several shards, run a secondary-index query, and confirm via query profiling that it fans out to every shard rather than a single one.
- The celebrity-hot-spot claim (§1, p219–220) is directly testable by construction: hash-partition a key-value store, direct a large volume of writes at a single key, and confirm all writes land on one partition/node regardless of hash function quality; then apply the random-suffix mitigation and confirm the writes spread across multiple partitions.
- The global-index asynchronous-staleness claim (§1, p223) is directly testable against a real system (e.g. DynamoDB): write an item, immediately query its global secondary index, and confirm the update is not always instantaneously visible.

## 9. Cross-references

- Directly extends Ch.5's replication material — explicitly stated as an independent, orthogonal concern that composes with partitioning without altering it. No contradiction found. `[S]`
- Directly extends Ch.3's B-tree and SSTable sorted-storage mechanics, reused both for within-partition ordering and as an explicit structural analogy for dynamic partition splitting/merging. `[S]`
- Forward-references (not yet synthesized in this vault): Ch.7 (distributed/multi-object transactions needed for consistent secondary-index maintenance and cross-partition writes), Ch.9 (consensus protocols underlying reliable partition-assignment agreement), and Ch.10 (parallel query execution for analytic/MPP workloads).
- No contradiction found with any already-synthesized source in this vault.

# Ch.7 — Transactions

**Source:** `ddia_kleppmann` (Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann, O'Reilly, 2017)
**PDF page range:** 235–286 (52 pages) — per `audit/CHAPTER_MAP.csv`
**Chapter map status:** `located`, `entry_type: chapter`
**Synthesis status:** `synthesized` (this session)
**Provenance key:** `[S]` source-supported · `[D]` derived interpretation · `[U]` unresolved

---

## 1. Concepts and definitions

**Transaction, defined and its purpose named directly [S]** (p236): "a way for an application to group several reads and writes together into a logical unit." Either "the entire transaction succeeds (commit) or it fails (abort, rollback)." Their purpose: "to simplify the programming model for applications accessing a database," letting applications "ignore certain potential error scenarios and concurrency issues, because the database takes care of them instead."

**ACID, the four letters individually redefined by the chapter with explicit caveats [S]** (p238–241): Atomicity is "not about concurrency" — it "describes what happens if a client wants to make several writes, but a fault occurs after some of the writes have been processed," with the guarantee being abortability: on failure, "the database must discard or undo any writes it has made so far." Consistency (p238–239) is "terribly overloaded" across three unrelated meanings (replica consistency, CAP-theorem linearizability, ACID's own "application-specific notion of the database being in a 'good state'") — the chapter's explicit verdict: "consistency (in the ACID sense) is a property of the application," not the database, "the letter C doesn't really belong in ACID." Isolation (p239–240) means "concurrently executing transactions are isolated from each other," formalized classically as serializability — "each transaction can pretend that it is the only transaction running on the entire database" — though "in practice, serializable isolation is rarely used" for performance reasons. Durability (p240) is "the promise that once a transaction has committed successfully, any data it has written will not be forgotten," acknowledging "perfect durability does not exist."

**ACID's marketing-term critique, an explicit named verdict [S]** (p237): "in practice, one database's implementation of ACID does not equal another's implementation."

Today (p238), when a system claims to be ACID compliant, it's unclear what guarantees you can actually expect — the chapter's own conclusion is that ACID has become mostly a marketing term. `[D]`

BASE (Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency) is named even vaguer (p238): its only sensible definition is simply not being ACID. `[D]`

**Replication's durability risks, six named concrete failure scenarios undermining a naive "just replicate" assumption [S]** (p240–241): a correlated fault (power outage, a crash-triggering bug) can take down all replicas simultaneously, losing in-memory-only data; asynchronous replication can lose recent writes when a leader fails; SSDs can silently violate their own guarantees on sudden power loss, "even fsync isn't guaranteed to work correctly"; storage-engine/filesystem interactions can corrupt files after a crash; data can gradually corrupt on disk undetected, contaminating replicas and recent backups alike; and a powered-off SSD can begin losing data within weeks depending on temperature.

**Single-object vs. multi-object operations, precisely distinguished [S]** (p243–246): multi-object transactions coordinate writes across several rows/documents/records — needed to keep foreign-key references valid, keep denormalized data in sync (the chapter's own worked email-unread-counter example), and keep secondary indexes consistent with the underlying data. Single-object atomicity/isolation is what "storage engines almost universally aim to provide" even without full transactions — implemented via a crash-recovery log (atomicity) and a per-object lock (isolation) — and single-object operations like atomic increment or compare-and-set are explicitly warned against being marketed as "lightweight transactions" or "ACID," since "a transaction is usually understood as a mechanism for grouping multiple operations on multiple objects into one unit of execution."

**Read committed, the chapter's own two-guarantee definition [S]** (p246–248): "you will only see data that has been committed (no dirty reads)" and "you will only overwrite data that has been committed (no dirty writes)." Dirty writes are prevented via row-level locks held until commit/abort; dirty reads are prevented not via read locks (which would let one long write block many reads) but by the database remembering both the old committed value and the new uncommitted value, serving the old value to concurrent readers until commit.

**Read skew (non-repeatable reads), defined via Alice's two-account worked example [S]** (p251): reading account balances at different points mid-transfer makes it "appears as though she only has a total of $900 in her accounts — it seems that $100 have vanished into thin air."

Read skew is considered acceptable under read committed isolation (p251), since "the account balances that Alice saw were indeed committed at the time when she read them" — but it is unacceptable for two named use cases: backups (a copy spanning hours can mix old and new data, creating a permanently inconsistent restore point) and long-running analytic/integrity-check queries, which "are likely to return nonsensical results if they observe parts of the database at different points in time" (p251).

**Snapshot isolation (MVCC), the chapter's own definition [S]** (p252): "each transaction reads from a consistent snapshot of the database, that is, all the data that was committed in the database at a particular point in time."

Its performance mantra (p252): "a key principle of snapshot isolation is readers never block writers, and writers never block readers."

Implemented by tagging every row with `created_by`/`deleted_by` transaction IDs and applying four explicit visibility rules (p254): ignore writes from transactions still in-progress at the reader's start time; ignore writes from aborted transactions; ignore writes from transactions with a later ID than the reader; show everything else. `[D]`

**The "repeatable read" naming confusion, an explicit named historical accident [S]** (p254–255): PostgreSQL and MySQL call their snapshot isolation implementation "repeatable read" purely to claim SQL-standard compliance, since the standard predates snapshot isolation and only defines a vaguer, ambiguous "repeatable read." Oracle calls its (weaker) snapshot isolation "serializable"; IBM DB2 uses "repeatable read" to mean actual serializability. Explicit verdict: "nobody really knows what repeatable read means."

**Lost update, defined via the read-modify-write-cycle pattern, with four named prevention techniques [S]** (p255–258): occurs when "two transactions do this concurrently, one of the modifications can be lost, because the second write does not include the first modification." Techniques: atomic write operations (best when applicable, e.g. `UPDATE counters SET value = value + 1`, implemented via cursor-stability locking); explicit application-level locking (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`) when built-in atomic operations aren't expressive enough; automatic lost-update detection (available in PostgreSQL repeatable read, Oracle serializable, SQL Server snapshot isolation, but explicitly not in MySQL/InnoDB repeatable read); and compare-and-set, with an explicit warning that it is only safe "if the database allows the WHERE clause to read from an old snapshot" it can silently fail to prevent the very race it's meant to stop.

**Write skew, defined via the on-call-doctors worked example [S]** (p260): "it is neither a dirty write nor a lost update, because the two transactions are updating two different objects"

Write skew generalizes lost update (p261): "you can think of write skew as a generalization of lost update. Write skew can occur if two transactions read the same objects, and then update some of those objects"

Four named real-world instances beyond the doctors example, synthesized from the chapter's own list (p263–264) `[D]`: meeting-room double-booking, multiplayer-game piece collisions, username-claiming races, and double-spending via concurrently-inserted spending items that individually look safe.

**Phantoms, the mechanism underlying write-skew's hardest cases [S]** (p264): "a write in one transaction changes the result of a search query in another transaction, is called a phantom"

Distinguished from the doctors case (p264): when the anomaly involves checking for the absence of rows, a row-level lock has nothing to attach to, since there is no existing row to lock — this is what makes phantom-driven write skew categorically harder than row-level lost updates. `[D]`

**Materializing conflicts, an explicit last-resort technique with a named ugliness verdict [S]** (p264): artificially pre-creating lock-target rows (e.g. a room × 15-minute-slot table) purely so phantoms have something concrete to lock. "It can be hard and error-prone to figure out how to materialize conflicts, and it's ugly to let a concurrency control mechanism leak into the application data model."

"For those reasons, materializing conflicts should be considered a last resort if no alternative is possible" (p264).

**Serializability, the chapter's own strongest-isolation definition [S]** (p265): "the end result is the same as if they had executed one at a time, serially, without any concurrency." Thus "the database prevents all possible race conditions" (p265).

The three named implementation techniques (p265): literal serial execution; two-phase locking (2PL), "for several decades... the only viable option"; and optimistic techniques such as serializable snapshot isolation (SSI).

**Actual serial execution, its two enabling changes and its stored-procedure requirement [S]** (p266–267): made viable circa 2007 by cheap-enough RAM to keep the active dataset in memory, plus the recognition that OLTP transactions are typically short. Because network round-trips between an interactive client and server would leave a single thread idle most of the time, serial-execution systems (VoltDB/H-Store, Redis, Datomic) require the entire transaction be submitted up front as a stored procedure rather than run interactively.

**Serial execution's partitioning-throughput trade-off, an explicit named hard limit [S]** (p269): partitioning lets each CPU core own its own partition and transaction thread, scaling linearly for single-partition transactions, but cross-partition transactions have additional coordination overhead.

VoltDB is named as achieving only (p269) "about 1,000 cross-partition writes per second."

This is (p269) "orders of magnitude below its single-partition transaction throughput, and cannot be increased by adding more machines"

**Two-phase locking (2PL), defined by its stronger-than-dirty-write-prevention lock rules [S]** (p270): readers use shared locks, writers use exclusive locks, and critically "a reader must also block a writer, and vice versa" — the direct inverse of snapshot isolation's mantra. The "two-phase" name comes from lock acquisition happening throughout execution (phase one) and all locks releasing together only at commit/abort (phase two). `[D]`

**2PL's named performance downside and its deadlock cost [S]** (p271): "transaction throughput and response times of queries are significantly worse under two-phase locking than under weak isolation." This is due to acquisition/release overhead and, more importantly, reduced concurrency — one slow or lock-heavy transaction can stall a whole queue with no upper wait bound, since traditional databases don't limit transaction duration. `[D]`

Deadlocks (p272) "occur much more frequently under 2PL serializable" — each one requiring a full transaction retry. `[D]`

**Predicate locks and their practical index-range-lock approximation [S]** (p272): a predicate lock conceptually attaches to "all objects that match some search condition," including objects that don't yet exist, solving the phantom problem.

Unfortunately (p273), "predicate locks do not perform well." The practical compromise, index-range locking, deliberately over-approximates the predicate by attaching a shared lock to an index entry or range — safe, "because any write that matches the original predicate will definitely also match the approximations" (p273) — falling back to a full-table lock if no suitable index exists.

**Serializable snapshot isolation (SSI), defined as an optimistic technique layered on ordinary snapshot isolation [S]** (p274): "optimistic in this context means that instead of blocking if something"

potentially dangerous happens, transactions continue anyway, in the hope that everything will turn out alright (p275). `[D]`

When a transaction wants to commit (p274), the database checks whether isolation was violated; if so, the transaction is aborted and has to be retried. First described in 2008; used in PostgreSQL (since 9.1) and, distributed, in FoundationDB.

**SSI's two named conflict-detection mechanisms [S]** (p276–278): detecting stale MVCC reads (a transaction's snapshot ignored a write that has since committed, invalidating any premise built on that read — deferred to commit time rather than the read itself, since a read-only transaction never needs to abort for this reason) and detecting writes that affect prior reads (index-range "lock" entries act as tripwires notifying, not blocking, other transactions when their previously-read data is later modified — whichever transaction commits first wins, the other aborts). `[D]`

**SSI's performance profile relative to the other two serializable techniques, an explicit named comparison [S]** (p278): "one transaction doesn't need to block waiting for locks held by another transaction" — readers and writers never block each other, giving predictable low-variance query latency.

Unlike serial execution (p279), SSI is not capped at one CPU core, since FoundationDB distributes conflict detection across machines. Its main sensitivity: high abort rates under long-running read-write transactions, since more time spent means more opportunity to conflict — but "SSI is probably less sensitive to slow transactions than two-phase locking or serial execution" (p279).

## 2. WHAT / WHY / WHEN

**WHAT:** the chapter's full taxonomy of transactional guarantees (ACID, precisely redefined) and concurrency-control mechanisms — from the weakest practical isolation level (read committed) through snapshot isolation to full serializability via three distinct implementation strategies — organized around a single recurring question: which named race conditions (dirty read, dirty write, read skew, lost update, write skew, phantom) does a given isolation level actually prevent. `[D]`

**WHY it matters:** transactions exist purely to let application developers "pretend that certain concurrency problems and certain kinds of hardware and software fault don't exist" (p279), collapsing a large space of partial-failure and race-condition bugs into a single "abort and retry" pattern — but the chapter's central warning is that most systems in practice use isolation levels weaker than full serializability, so knowing exactly which anomalies a chosen isolation level does *not* prevent is a prerequisite for reasoning correctly about an application's actual safety, not an academic nicety. `[D]`

**WHEN to accept weaker isolation vs. pay for serializability, synthesized across the chapter (p246–284):** read committed suffices when only dirty reads/writes are a risk and the application never makes a decision based on a query result that must still hold true at commit time; snapshot isolation is right for long-running read-only workloads (backups, analytics) and moderate write conflict, but explicitly does not protect against write skew or phantom-driven anomalies (double-booking, double-spending, uniqueness-adjacent races) — those require either explicit `SELECT FOR UPDATE` locking, a unique constraint if the invariant reduces to one, or true serializable isolation (2PL, serial execution, or SSI) when the invariant spans multiple objects/rows.

## 3. Assumptions and prerequisites

- Directly extends Ch.5's replication material for the durability discussion (asynchronous replication's write-loss risk) and for conflict resolution's connection to lost updates in multi-leader/leaderless systems. `[S]` (p241, p258)
- Directly extends Ch.6's partitioning material for the serial-execution throughput discussion (single-partition vs. cross-partition transaction cost) and the secondary-index cross-partition coordination cost. `[S]` (p271)
- Directly extends Ch.3's storage-engine internals (write-ahead logging for atomicity, B-tree structures reused by append-only/copy-on-write MVCC implementations like CouchDB/Datomic/LMDB). `[S]` (p236, p254–255)
- Forward-references distributed transactions, two-phase commit (2PC, explicitly distinguished from 2PL), and generalizing single-node serializability techniques to distributed databases, all to Ch.9 — not yet synthesized in this vault. `[D]`

## 4. Mechanism / key steps

**Snapshot isolation's MVCC visibility check, the chapter's own worked PostgreSQL-style description (p252–253)** `[D]`: every row carries `created_by` and `deleted_by` transaction-ID fields, never overwritten in place — an update becomes an internal delete-plus-create pair → at transaction start, the database snapshots the set of in-progress transaction IDs → on read, a row is visible only if its creator committed before the reader started and (if deleted) its deleter had not committed before the reader started → garbage collection later reclaims rows no longer visible to any active transaction.

**Two-phase locking's shared/exclusive lock protocol, the chapter's own worked description (p273)** `[D]`: a transaction wanting to read acquires a shared lock (compatible with other shared locks, blocked by any exclusive lock); a transaction wanting to write acquires an exclusive lock (blocked by any existing lock, shared or exclusive); a read-then-write transaction upgrades shared to exclusive; every lock, once acquired, is held until the transaction's final commit or abort — never released early — which is the "two-phase" structure (acquisition phase, then release phase).

**SSI's dual-detection commit-time check, the chapter's own worked two-doctor example (p281–283)** `[D]`: a transaction reads from an ordinary MVCC snapshot as usual → the database separately tracks (a) which in-progress transactions' writes were ignored due to visibility rules, and (b) which other transactions have read data that this transaction's own writes are now modifying → at commit time, if either tracked condition indicates the read transaction's premise may now be false, the transaction is aborted and must be retried → only transactions that pass this check are allowed to commit, guaranteeing the result matches some serial execution order.

## 5. Trade-offs and limitations

- **Weak isolation levels (read committed, snapshot isolation) perform far better than serializable isolation but leave the application responsible for detecting and preventing lost updates, write skew, and phantoms (§1, p249, p260–265):** the chapter frames this as the central practical trade-off of the entire chapter — performance bought at the cost of correctness reasoning being pushed onto the application developer.
- **Two-phase locking guarantees full serializability but at a severe, unbounded-latency performance cost under contention, with deadlocks adding further wasted retry work (§1, p273–274):** a direct, named cost the chapter credits as the historical reason weak isolation levels proliferated despite their correctness gaps.
- **Serial execution eliminates concurrency-control overhead entirely but caps throughput at a single CPU core (or requires perfect partitioning), and cross-partition transactions remain orders of magnitude slower than single-partition ones (§1, p267, p271):** the trade-off is structural, not tunable — it only works when the workload is genuinely small-and-fast or cleanly partitionable.
- **Serializable snapshot isolation avoids blocking entirely (unlike 2PL) and isn't capped at one core (unlike serial execution), but its abort rate rises with transaction duration and contention, making it a poor fit for long-running read-write transactions (§1, p284–285):** SSI is explicitly framed as the newest and most promising of the three, but not a strictly dominant replacement — its performance is workload-dependent in a different way than the other two.

## 6. Failure modes and edge cases

- **Read skew corrupting backups and analytic queries, a concrete named consequence distinct from the transient case (§1, p250):** unlike Alice's temporarily-vanished $100 (which reappears on refresh), a backup or long-running integrity check that captures pre- and post-transfer state simultaneously bakes the inconsistency in permanently — "if you need to restore from such a backup, the inconsistencies... become permanent."
- **Compare-and-set silently failing to prevent lost updates on a stale snapshot (§1, p258):** "if the database allows the `WHERE` clause to read from an old snapshot, this statement may not prevent lost updates, because the condition may be true even though another concurrent write is occurring" — a concrete, named case where a technique marketed as a safe primitive is unsafe depending on implementation.
- **Phantom-driven write skew defeating row-level locking entirely (§1, p264–265):** in the meeting-room, username-claiming, and double-spending examples, the anomaly involves checking for the *absence* of a matching row, so there is no existing row for `SELECT FOR UPDATE` to lock — a structurally different and harder failure mode than the doctors example, requiring index-range locks or materialized conflict rows instead.
- **Retrying a transaction that actually succeeded, causing a duplicate side effect (§1, p249, the abort-handling discussion):** if the network fails while the server is acknowledging a successful commit, the client retries a transaction that already took effect — "unless you have an additional application-level deduplication mechanism in place," this silently double-applies the operation (e.g. sending a duplicate email, deferred explicitly to Ch.9's 2PC discussion for cross-system side effects).
- **Retrying under overload making things worse, a named anti-pattern [S]** (p246): "if the error is due to overload, retrying the transaction will make the problem worse, not better." This motivates limited retries, exponential backoff, and distinguishing overload errors from other transient errors. `[D]`

## 7. Implications for design / build / maintain / RCA / optimization

- **Design:** the isolation-level decision framework (§2) is directly reusable for choosing a transaction isolation level for any new schema/workload in this vault's projects — explicitly check whether the application's invariants span multiple rows (write-skew risk) before assuming snapshot isolation or read committed is sufficient. `[D]`
- **Build:** the atomic-operation-first hierarchy (§1, p255–256: atomic operations > explicit locking > automatic lost-update detection > compare-and-set with its stated caveat) is a directly reusable decision order for implementing any read-modify-write cycle safely.
- **Maintain:** the "data outlives code"-adjacent replication-durability checklist (§1, p240–241) is a directly reusable pre-mortem checklist when auditing whether a system's durability claims actually hold under correlated faults, SSD power loss, or silent disk corruption.
- **RCA:** an observed "impossible" data inconsistency (e.g. an invariant spanning multiple rows silently violated, or denormalized data drifting out of sync) is directly diagnosable against the write-skew and phantom patterns (§1, §6) before assuming an application logic bug — check whether the isolation level in use actually prevents that specific anomaly class.
- **Optimization:** the three-way serializability-technique trade-off (§1, §5: serial execution vs. 2PL vs. SSI) is a directly reusable framework for choosing a concurrency-control strategy under a known workload shape — favor serial execution for small in-memory partitionable workloads, SSI for read-heavy or low-contention workloads needing full serializability without 2PL's blocking cost, and 2PL only when neither alternative is available or contention is genuinely severe enough that optimistic retry overhead would dominate.

## 8. How to test / verify these claims

- The lost-update race condition (§1, p239, Figure 7-1) is directly reproducible: run two concurrent read-modify-write counter-increment transactions against a database at read committed isolation and confirm the final counter value undercounts the true number of increments.
- The read-skew anomaly (§1, p249–250) is directly reproducible: run a concurrent funds-transfer transaction against a two-account balance read at read committed isolation, timing the reads to straddle the transfer, and confirm the observed total is transiently wrong.
- The write-skew anomaly (§1, p260–261) is directly reproducible using the chapter's own doctors example: run two concurrent "go off-call if 2+ on call" transactions under snapshot isolation and confirm both succeed, leaving zero doctors on call.
- The automatic lost-update detection claim (§1, p256) is directly testable by comparing behavior across databases: run the same concurrent counter read-modify-write cycle under PostgreSQL's repeatable read (should abort one transaction) versus MySQL/InnoDB's repeatable read (should silently lose the update, per the chapter's explicit claim).
- The SSI abort-under-contention claim (§1, p283) is directly testable: run many concurrent conflicting read-write transactions against a PostgreSQL database at serializable isolation (its SSI implementation) and measure the abort rate as contention increases.

## 9. Cross-references

- Directly extends Ch.5's replication durability and conflict-resolution material — read committed/snapshot isolation lost-update prevention explicitly does not carry over to multi-leader/leaderless replicated systems, which instead rely on sibling-merging (Ch.5's own mechanism). No contradiction found. `[S]`
- Directly extends Ch.6's partitioning material for the serial-execution and cross-partition transaction cost discussion. No contradiction found. `[S]`
- Directly extends Ch.3's storage-engine internals (WAL for atomicity; B-tree append-only/copy-on-write variants reused by MVCC implementations). No contradiction found. `[S]`
- Forward-references (not yet synthesized in this vault): Ch.9 for distributed transactions, two-phase commit (2PC, explicitly distinguished from 2PL), and generalizing this chapter's single-node serializability techniques across multiple nodes; Ch.8 for network-unreliability context underlying the "retry after ambiguous failure" discussion.
- No contradiction found with any already-synthesized source in this vault.
